title: I Am the Son of One Who Stands Revealed, a Climber of Passes
intro: Al-Asma'i tells how al-Akhwas and al-Ubayrid sent Suhaym a challenge in verse. Staff in hand, the older poet walked up and down the valley composing his reply. He makes experience tangible in a camel’s teeth, a second yield of milk and the splinters of a spear shaft. Al-Hajjaj later took the opening of his address in Kufa from this poem.

translation: I am the son of one who stands revealed, a climber of passes.
When I lay my turban down, you will know me.
1.sharh: His standing is plain and he has made his way up difficult passes. The gesture with the turban turns an abstract claim about reputation into a moment when everyone can see his face.

translation: Our place among Himyari’s people
is the lion’s place in the heart of the thicket.
2.sharh: Himyari is the ancestor of his own branch of Riyah. A lion in the very middle of its cover seems as secure in its place as Suhaym feels among his people.

translation: My match never comes back to face me
on the return day without a companion,
3.sharh: One encounter teaches his opponent to bring help. Two near-identical words distinguish the man who takes him on from the companion that man must bring next time.

translation: a maned lion the riders turn aside from,
whose kill none approaches for a long while.
4.sharh: Even the ally his opponent needs is lion-like. Travellers give him room on the road and leave his kill alone, two measures of the fear his presence inspires.

translation: I would excuse full-grown camels for challenging me.
What have I to do with a pair of yearlings?
5.sharh: Older camels with their mature teeth make worthy competitors. Giving the two challengers the name for calves in their second year tells them exactly where he ranks them.

translation: What advantage can the poets steal over me
now I have passed the far end of forty?
6.sharh: The poets would have to stalk him as a hunter stalks game. Experience, he implies, lets him recognise their manoeuvre while they still think themselves unseen.

translation: Fifty years old, with all my strength gathered,
I have cut my teeth on the handling of affairs.
7.sharh: Fifty is the point at which his powers have come together. The word for being seasoned by experience also evokes molars, recalling the mature camels of his challenge.

translation: Even my second yield, my running through a year,
would tax a youngster of doubtful promise.
8.sharh: His rivals had boasted of their first burst of speed. He answers with what he has left in reserve, like milk still to be drawn at a second milking.

translation: I shall live as long as life is mine, my back
resting against a support I can trust.
9.sharh: He can spend the rest of his life upright because his back is supported. Behind the figure of stacked household goods is the dependable weight of his kin.

translation: Noble on my mother’s side, of Riyah on either side,
I have a brow bright as a sword blade.
10.sharh: He gives his maternal kin a share in the honour just claimed. A visible brightness, like polished steel catching the light, carries the boast back to the uncovered face of the opening.

translation: Our spear shaft bristles with splinters.
It pulls hard at the neck of anyone who grapples with it.
11.sharh: A man who lays hold of the shaft gets splinters in his hand and feels a pull on his own neck. Suhaym ends with what challenging his family feels like on the challenger’s side.

1.1.2-3.meaning: “Son of one who stands revealed”, a man whose distinction is plain to see.

1.1.4-5.head: طَلّاعُ الثَّنايا
1.1.4-5.meaning: “Climber of passes”, someone tried on steep ground and in difficult undertakings.

1.2.3.head: عِمامَة
1.2.3.meaning: A turban, the headwrap he lays aside as he promises recognition.

2.1.4.head: حِميَرِيّ
2.1.4.meaning: Himyari ibn Riyah ibn Yarbu', the Tamimi ancestor of Suhaym’s clan.

2.2.5.head: عَرين
2.2.5.meaning: A lion’s lair in dense cover.

3.1.5.head: قِرن
3.1.5.meaning: An opponent matched with a man in contest.

3.2.2.head: غِبّ
3.2.2.meaning: Watering on alternate days, here a return after an interval.

4.1.1-2.head: ذو لِبَد
4.1.1-2.meaning: “The maned one”, a lion with thick hair round its neck.

4.2.3.head: فَريسَة
4.2.3.meaning: An animal killed and claimed by a predator.

5.1.2.head: بازِل
5.1.2.meaning: A fully mature camel whose canine tooth has come through.

5.1.5.head: خاطَرَ
5.1.5.meaning: Challenged or competed against someone with stakes at risk.

5.2.4-5.head: اِبنا لَبون
5.2.4-5.meaning: “Two calves of milk-giving mothers”, males in their second year whose dams have calved again.

6.1.2.head: اِدَّرى
6.1.2.meaning: Stalked game so as to take it unawares.

7.2.1.head: نَجَّذَ
7.2.1.meaning: Seasoned someone through experience. The word suggests cutting one’s back teeth.

8.1.2.head: عُلالَة
8.1.2.meaning: A second yield of milk, hence energy left over after a first effort.

8.1.3.head: جِراء
8.1.3.meaning: A trial of speed, echoing the challengers’ own word.

8.2.4-5.head: الضَّرَع الظَّنون
8.2.4-5.meaning: “The untried weakling”, a young competitor whose powers remain doubtful.

9.2.3.head: نَضَد
9.2.3.meaning: A stand on which goods are piled, here the backing his family gives him.

10.1.4.head: سَلَف
10.1.4.meaning: A forebear. The dual reaches back along two lines of descent.

10.1.5.head: رِياح
10.1.5.meaning: Riyah, Suhaym’s people, a branch of Yarbu' within Tamim.

11.1.2.head: قَناة
11.1.2.meaning: The wooden shaft of a spear, here standing for the clan.

11.1.3.head: مَشِظ
11.1.3.meaning: Rough with splinters that stick in the hand.

11.1.4.head: شَظاً
11.1.4.meaning: Slivers that break from the shaft.
